name: PFL to PFW ratio

card.summary: An eye-shape metric comparing palpebral fissure length (horizontal eye opening) to width/height, used in looksmaxxing to judge eye-area harmony and to decide what eye-area changes to pursue.
card.note: Community-defined ratio; target values are stated by forum users and are not clinical norms.

quick.overview:
PFL to PFW compares how wide the eye opening is horizontally with how tall it is vertically. The palpebral fissure is the space between the open eyelids, and looksmaxxing users treat the ratio as a way to describe eye shape, with higher ratios reading as longer, narrower eyes.

On looksmax.org, one thread states a good ratio is about 3:1 and an ideal around 3.5:1 with an average length of 28 to 30 mm. Clinical sources give typical adult measurements of roughly 30 mm by 10 mm, which falls in the same region. No published study has tested the forum's ideal values.
quick.how: People measure or estimate the horizontal and vertical eye opening from photos, compute the ratio, and compare it with the community target. Discussed ways to change it include lower eyelid position, scleral show, squinting, and eyelid or canthal surgery.
quick.risks: The metric itself carries no risk. Eyelid and canthal surgery have the usual surgical risks, and unusual eyelid measurements can sometimes be linked with medical conditions that a clinician evaluates.

lead: PFL to PFW ratio, short for palpebral fissure length to palpebral fissure width (or height), is a measure of eye shape used in looksmaxxing communities. The palpebral fissure is the elliptical opening between the upper and lower eyelids, bounded by the medial and lateral canthi.[1]

Users on looksmax.org describe the ratio as a major component of eye-area appearance. One thread states a good ratio is around 3:1 and an ideal about 3.5:1, and that the ratio matters more than raw length as long as length is average, quoted there as 28 to 30 mm.[2] Standard references give adult averages of about 30 mm horizontally and 10 mm vertically, a ratio near 3:1.[1]

The thread suggests that an unfavourable ratio can be improved by raising the lower eyelid, for example where sclera shows because of lower lid retraction, or by squinting.[2] No published study has tested the ideal values proposed in the community.

chain: Measure horizontal vs vertical eye opening
Compare against the community target ratio
Choose eyelid position or styling changes to move toward it
angle.text: Proponents use the ratio to diagnose which part of the eye area looks off, such as a tall opening that reads as rounder. They then focus on lower lid position, sclera show and squinting as levers, or consider eyelid surgery.

infobox: Horizontal eye opening divided by vertical opening
Canthal tilt, scleral show, lower lid retraction

paras: The palpebral fissure length is measured between the lateral and medial canthi, and width (height) is the vertical distance between upper and lower lid margins at the centre. In adults the fissure is about 10 mm tall and 30 mm long.[1]

The ratio is invoked on looksmax.org as part of eye-area analysis alongside canthal tilt and eyelid exposure. A widely read thread calls it extremely important, describing a high-ratio eye as more harmonious and a low-ratio eye as rounder, and says the ratio can be improved only via lower eyelid retraction correction or squinting.[2] Other users in the thread questioned the 3.5:1 figure.[2]

Clinicians use fissure dimensions in dysmorphology: reduced horizontal width is seen in fetal alcohol syndrome and Williams syndrome, and increased vertical height in conditions including Graves' disease, where lid retraction is known as Dalrymple's sign.[1]
No studies found. Clinical literature measures palpebral fissure dimensions in syndromes and across populations, but no study has examined a PFL to PFW ratio as an attractiveness target.

lore.intro: The ratio is discussed on looksmax.org as an eye-area metric with numerical targets.[2]

claims.claim: A 3:1 to 3.5:1 PFL to PFW ratio is good to ideal
claims.believers: Thread authors say a fissure about three to three and a half times wider than tall gives a harmonious, attractive eye, and that a poor ratio can undermine the whole eye area.[2]
claims.experts: Reference sources report typical adult fissures near 30 by 10 mm; no published study has tested a preferred ratio.[1]

claims.claim: A poor ratio can be improved by lower eyelid position or squinting
claims.believers: The thread says raising the lower lid, where scleral show exists, or squinting may help.[2]
claims.experts: No published studies have tested squinting for this purpose.

refs.title: Redpill PFL to PFW ratio is extremely important
